abstract: We extend full conformal prediction to nonexchangeable data and nonsymmetric model fitting, with related split conformal and jackknife+ procedures. Prespecified calibration weights in [0,1] reduce reliance on observations considered less comparable to the test point, while fixed algorithm tags allow fitting to use order or regression weights. A data-independent swap, sampled with probabilities proportional to these weights and a unit test weight, makes miscoverage imply membership in a high-residual set of normalized weight at most alpha. Comparing swapped and original residual distributions then gives finite-sample coverage at least 1-alpha minus their weighted total-variation distances, without requiring fitting symmetry. Exchangeability eliminates this penalty; under nonexchangeability, a small penalty bounds undercoverage, with distinct residuals and small normalized test weight additionally limiting overcoverage. Experiments distinguish calibration from fitting: on ordered electricity data, residual weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas weighted least squares narrows intervals while retaining the coverage improvement. Random permutation removes this width advantage, and election coverage improves but remains below the 90% target. Thus the guarantee depends on residual-distribution changes, while empirical benefits depend on the evaluated ordering and weighting choices.
methods: Theorem 2b fixes calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags before observing data. Normalize the weights with a unit test weight and draw K independently using these probabilities. At the true label, fitting after swapping observations K and n+1 while keeping tags fixed puts the test residual at index K of R(Z^K). For any residual vector r, indices S(r) strictly above its weighted (1-alpha)-quantile have normalized weight at most alpha. Because the test weight dominates every calibration weight, the prediction cutoff with test mass at infinity is no smaller than the cutoff for R(Z^K); miscoverage therefore implies K belongs to S(R(Z^K)). Independence expresses this event probability as a weighted sum over K. Replacing each swapped residual law by the original costs at most its total-variation distance. The original-law sum is at most alpha, yielding miscoverage at most alpha plus the weighted residual-distribution penalty.
results: Table 2 shows that, on ordered electricity data, improving coverage through calibration weighting need not require wider intervals once fitting also changes. At a 90% target, ordinary full conformal with least squares (CP+LS) averages 85.2% coverage and width 0.565. Weighting only calibration residuals (NexCP+LS) raises coverage to 89.0% but increases width to 0.606. Adding weighted least-squares fitting (NexCP+WLS) retains higher coverage, 89.3%, while reducing width to 0.527, below both alternatives; neither weighted method reaches 90% on average. Uniform random permutation makes the data exchangeable: the respective coverages are 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8%, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663. The fitting change thus offers no width advantage in this control, and weighted procedures have greater variability. This contrast supports distinct calibration and fitting benefits in the ordered setting, not a generally narrower weighted method. These averages across prediction times neither establish coverage at every time nor universal 90% coverage under drift, because the theorem's weighted swapped-residual total-variation penalty may be large.
notes: Keep theoretical and empirical claims distinct: the WLS experiment cites equation (14), not the randomized-swap procedure (20); confirm whether the implementation includes the swap before attributing its results to Theorem 2b. Table 2 reports temporal averages without uncertainty estimates or interval-width units; retain descriptive comparisons, not significance claims. The residual total-variation penalty is not empirically quantified. Jackknife+ has a 1-2alpha baseline guarantee, unlike split and full conformal. Two-sided near-nominal coverage additionally requires distinct residuals and a small normalized test weight. The ordered/permuted comparison separates calibration's coverage tradeoff from fitting's setting-dependent width benefit.
